title_en: Shanghai Huangpu District People's Procuratorate v. Meng Dong and He Likang — online theft case
ruling_gist_en: 1. Electronic documents collected in accordance with statutory procedures, if relevant to the case and capable of objectively reflecting the true circumstances of the case when corroborated with other evidence, may legally serve as evidence in criminal proceedings.
keywords_en: Criminal; Theft; First instance; Basic People's Court; Shanghai; Natural person; Criminal Law; Whether virtual property constitutes an object of theft; Probative value of electronic evidence; Determination of the amount of theft; Distinction between completed and attempted offense; Partial support; Online theft; Virtual property; Q coins; Game points cards; Hacker intrusion; Theft
full_text_en:
Shanghai Huangpu District People's Procuratorate v. Meng Dong and He Likang — online theft case

[Ruling Summary]

1. An electronic document collected in accordance with statutory procedures may serve as evidence in criminal proceedings if it is relevant to the case and, when corroborated with other evidence, can objectively reflect the true circumstances of the case.

2. If a virtual act committed by a person through a network causes harm to an object protected by criminal law in real life and constitutes a crime, that person shall be subject to criminal punishment.

3. Where the secret theft of virtual property in a network environment constitutes the crime of theft, the amount of the theft shall be determined according to the amount of loss in actual property corresponding to that virtual property in real life. The amount of the actual property corresponding to the virtual property in real life may be determined by the actual transaction price of that virtual property in real life.

4. The object of the crime of theft is a wide variety of public and private property. The methods for determining whether a theft is completed or attempted may differ depending on the type of property stolen. In judicial practice, there is no single, specific standard for determining an attempted theft in every case. Whether a theft is attempted shall be determined based on the three conditions set forth in Article 23 of the Criminal Law — "commencement of the criminal act," "failure to accomplish the crime," and "failure to accomplish the crime due to reasons beyond the criminal's will" — in conjunction with the specific circumstances, such as the type of property stolen. Where an actor steals another person's virtual property in a network, as long as the theft has achieved illegal possession of the victim's property corresponding to that virtual property in real life, the crime shall be deemed completed. Whether the actor ultimately disposes of the stolen property, or whether the victim subsequently recovers the virtual property, has no bearing on the completed criminal form of the actor.

Prosecutor: Shanghai Huangpu District People's Procuratorate.

Defendant: Meng Dong, male, 24 years old, native of Jiexiu City, Shanxi Province. Arrested on September 23, 2005. Prior to arrest, he was a computer maintenance technician at Guangzhou Modern Hardware Products Co., Ltd., Guangdong Province.

Defendant: He Likang, male, 22 years old, native of Jiexiu City, Shanxi Province. Arrested on September 23, 2005. Prior to arrest, he was an administrator of the Fourth Space Network Center in Taiyuan City, Shanxi Province.

The Shanghai Huangpu District People's Procuratorate filed a public prosecution against the defendants Meng Dong and He Likang for the crime of theft with the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court.

Indictment Allegations: The defendant Meng Dong stole the account numbers and passwords of the aggrieved unit, Shanghai Maoli Industrial Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Maoli Company"), and provided them to the defendant He Likang. The two conspired that Meng Dong would collect payments from buyers via online banking, while He Likang would intrude into Maoli Company's online top-up system to steal Q coins and then top up the QQ numbers of buyers informed by Meng Dong. From 18:32 on July 22, 2005, to 10:52 on the following day, He Likang stole a total of 32,298 Q coins, worth RMB 24,869.46, and 134 game point cards of 50 points and 60 of 100 points, worth RMB 1,079.50, from Maoli Company's account. Meng Dong and He Likang, with the intent of illegal possession, jointly and secretly stole property belonging to others totaling RMB 25,948.96 through a network system. The amount stolen was huge. Their conduct has violated the provisions of Article 264 of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Criminal Law"), constituting the crime of theft. It is requested that the criminal liability of the two defendants be investigated according to law. After the case was uncovered, the families of the two defendants helped to make full restitution of the stolen money. He Likang has circumstances of voluntary surrender and meritorious service, which may result in a lighter punishment according to law.

The prosecutor read out in court the report of the aggrieved unit, the inspection opinion issued by the public security organ after examining the two computer hard drives used by Meng Dong, and the QQ chat records exported from those hard drives. Evidence was presented, including the business licenses, contracts, payment vouchers and invoices of the aggrieved unit and related business units, photographs of the two computer hard drives seized from Meng Dong, and the bank card used by Meng Dong to receive the stolen money.

Defendants Meng Dong and He Likang did not raise objections to the facts alleged in the indictment. Defense counsels for the two defendants argued that the secret theft charged in the indictment was a virtual act occurring in a network environment. As is well known, many online games in which numerous netizens participate are filled with a large number of virtual killings and violent scenarios. If secret theft committed virtually in a network environment should be punished, then should virtual killings and violent acts also be investigated for criminal liability as intentional homicide or intentional injury? The answer is negative. Virtual acts are not criminal acts subject to criminal prosecution under criminal law; virtual acts do not cause harmful results in real life. Q coins and game point cards are both virtual property in online games and are not state-owned property, property collectively owned by the working masses, or private property of citizens protected by criminal law. Therefore, whether the secret theft of virtual property by the two defendants constitutes a criminal act to be punished under criminal law requires theoretical discussion. Secondly, Article 46 of the Criminal Procedure Law of the People's Republic of China (hereinafter "Criminal Procedure Law") provides: "In making a judgment on any case, emphasis must be placed on evidence, investigation and study; credence must not be given to confessions lightly. If there is only a defendant's confession and no other evidence, the defendant cannot be found guilty and sentenced. If there is no defendant's confession but the evidence is sufficient and reliable, the defendant may be found guilty and sentenced." Although this case has both defendants' confessions and other evidence, much of the other evidence consists of electronic documents. Electronic documents differ from traditional physical originals. Electronic documents have the characteristic of being easily copied, modified, and deleted; they lack the uniqueness and objectivity required for evidence, cannot fully reflect objective facts, and should not be used as valid evidence. If these electronic documents are excluded, the evidence in this case is not sufficient and reliable. Furthermore, although electronic documents can show which computer terminal they came from, a computer terminal cannot be directly equated with the user of that terminal. Therefore, these electronic documents cannot prove that they were created under the operation of the two defendants and cannot exclude the possibility that other users accidentally used that terminal to create these electronic documents; a conclusive exclusionary conclusion is impossible. Additionally, the value of Q coins and game point cards in real life is uncertain, as no authoritative institution has appraised it. The finding that the two defendants' actions caused huge losses to the aggrieved unit lacks basis. Even if the two defendants' conduct constitutes a crime, because the aggrieved unit and the network service provider discovered it in time and recovered some Q coins, that part of the crime was in an attempted state. After the case was uncovered, the families of the two defendants helped to make restitution of the stolen money. Therefore, the social harmfulness of the two defendants is relatively minor. Defendant He Likang also has circumstances of voluntary surrender and meritorious service. Thus, a mitigated punishment and probation are recommended for the two defendants.

Facts Found by the Shanghai Huangpu District People's Court:

The aggrieved unit, Maoli Company, became an agent for online sales of Tencent Q coins and NetEase Yikatong in Shanghai by entering into contracts with Tencent Technology (Beijing) Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "Tencent Company") and Guangzhou NetEase Computer System Co., Ltd. (hereinafter "NetEase Company").

In June-July 2005, the defendant Meng Dong, using a hacker program on the Internet in Guangzhou, stole the account numbers and passwords used by Maoli Company to log into Tencent and NetEase's online top-up systems. On the afternoon of July 22 of the same year, Meng Dong contacted the defendant He Likang through online chat, provided He Likang with the said stolen account numbers and passwords, and the two conspired to intrude into Maoli Company's online top-up system, steal Q coins and game point cards, and then sell them at low prices online.

At approximately 18:00 on July 22, 2005, the defendant Meng Dong first had the defendant He Likang attempt to top up 1 Q coin for his own QQ number. After confirming that the attempt was successful, Meng Dong found buyers and negotiated prices, then instructed He Likang to top up Q coins for the buyers' QQ numbers, requiring the buyers to transfer money to his Industrial and Commercial Bank of China Peony Card (card number 9558823602001916770, hereinafter "Card No. 770"). From 18:32 on July 22, 2005, to 10:52 on the following day, He Likang successively stole 32,298 Q coins worth RMB 24,869.46 from Maoli Company's account. In addition to topping up Q coins for buyers according to Meng Dong's instructions, he also topped up varying amounts of Q coins for his own and his friends' QQ numbers. From 00:25 to 04:07 on July 23, 2005, He Likang also successively stole 134 game point cards of 50 points and 60 of 100 points, worth RMB 1,079.50, from Maoli Company's account. The total value of Q coins and game point cards stolen by the two defendants was RMB 25,948.96.

After discovering the theft, the aggrieved unit, Maoli Company, immediately recovered 15,019 stolen Q coins online through Tencent Company. Maoli Company's actual loss was 17,279 Q coins, worth RMB 13,304.83. Including the stolen game point cards, Maoli Company's total loss was RMB 14,384.33.

After the defendants Meng Dong and He Likang were brought to justice, their families respectively paid RMB 8,000 and RMB 26,000 to offset the stolen money. The investigative authority returned RMB 14,384.33 to Maoli Company and returned the surplus to the payers.

The above facts are confirmed by the following evidence examined in court:

1. *Tencent Online Q Coin Primary Agent Sales Contract*, proving that Maoli Company became an agent for online sales of Tencent Q coins in Shanghai by entering into a contract with Tencent Company on July 1, 2005.

2. *Bank Transfer Vouchers*, proving that Maoli Company remitted RMB 300,000 and RMB 117,600 respectively to Tencent Company via China Merchants Bank on June 27 and July 29, 2005, for the purchase of Q coins.

3. *Invoices*, proving that Tencent Company collected RMB 417,600 remitted by Maoli Company under the name of information fees on August 5, 2005.

4. *Screenshots of Web Pages Downloaded from Computer*, proving that Tencent Company transferred 389,610 Q coins (valued at RMB 299,999.69) into Maoli Company's mlsoft account via the Internet on July 1, 2005.

5. *NetEase Online Direct Top-up System Agency Cooperation Agreement*, proving that Maoli Company became the general sales agent for NetEase Yikatong online direct top-up system in Shanghai by entering into an agreement with NetEase Company on July 1, 2004, purchasing at 82% of the face value of the online direct top-up cards.

6. *Telegraphic Transfer Vouchers*, proving that Maoli Company remitted RMB 42,500 to NetEase Company via China Minsheng Bank on July 20, 2005, for the purchase of game point cards.

7. *Invoices*, proving that NetEase Company collected RMB 4.25 million remitted by Maoli Company under the name of online service fees on August 7, 2005.

8. *Screenshots of Web Pages Downloaded from Computer*, proving that NetEase Company transferred 10,000 game point cards of 50 points into Maoli Company's mlsoft account on July 20, 2005.

9. *Testimony of Witness Xu Weixiong on July 25, 2005*, proving that from the evening of July 22, 2005, to the morning of the following day, 32,298 virtual Q coins were stolen from the Shanghai general agent account of Maoli Company's Tencent online system, and these Q coins were successively topped up into dozens of different QQ accounts; in the early morning of July 23, 2005, 134 NetEase game cards of 50 points and 60 of 100 points were stolen from the company's NetEase online system agent account, and these game cards were successively topped up into three game accounts. Q coins were purchased by the company from Tencent Company at RMB 0.77 each, with an online sales price of RMB 1 each. Game cards were purchased by the company from NetEase Company at RMB 4.25 per 50 points, with an online sales price of RMB 5 per 50 points.

10. *Screenshots of Maoli Company's mlsoft Account Sales Report and Tencent Company's mlsoft Account Top-up Records*, proving that 32,298 Q coins were stolen from the Tencent online top-up system within Maoli Company's mlsoft account during the period from 18:32 on July 22, 2005, to 10:52 on the following day.

11. *Written Testimony of Tencent Company*, proving that after being informed of the theft of 32,298 Q coins from Maoli Company, Tencent Company helped recover 15,019 Q coins by means of freezing.

12. *Testimony of Witness Zhong Jiadong on February 22, 2006*, proving that one day after the incident, after receiving a call from the aggrieved unit Maoli Company requesting an inquiry, Tencent Company found that the IP address of the computer terminal that logged into the Tencent online sales platform mlsoft account during the crime period of July 22 to the following day was 202.97.144.230.

13. *Screenshots of mlsoft Account Records Provided Respectively by Maoli Company and NetEase Company*, proving that from 23:59 on July 22, 2005, to 04:07 on July 23, 2005, a computer user with IP address 202.97.144.230 logged into Maoli Company's mlsoft account and transferred 134 game point cards of 50 points and 60 of 100 points from that account into the accounts of Yin Wei and others.

14. *Certificate Issued by the Public Information Network Security Supervision Detachment of the Taiyuan City Public Security Bureau, Shanxi Province*, confirming that the computer terminal with IP address 202.97.144.230 was located at "Fourth Space Network Center," Unit 6, Building H1, Qiaodong New Street, Yingze District, Taiyuan City.

15. *Search Records, List of Seized Items, and Photocopies of Photos of Seized Computer Hard Drives*, proving that a Seagate 80G S/N: 5JV880RK computer hard drive used by Meng Dong and Card No. 770 were seized by the Huangpu Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau at the residence of Meng Dong's girlfriend on September 5, 2005.

16. *Search Records, List of Seized Items, and Photocopies of Photos of Seized Computer Hard Drives*, proving that a Maxtor 40GB S/N: E1S60LXEZ9999 computer hard drive used by Meng Dong was seized by the Huangpu Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau at Guangzhou Modern Hardware Products Co., Ltd. on September 5, 2005.

17. *Inspection Opinion Issued by the Public Information Network Security Supervision Division of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau*, proving that:
   ① From the computer hard drive (S/N: E1S60LXEZ9999) seized at Meng Dong's workplace, a file named "important.txt" was retrieved, containing the account numbers and passwords of the aggrieved unit Maoli Company; chat records between Meng Dong (QQ No. 12290018, nickname "Doudou") and He Liangliang (He Likang's brother, QQ No. 75475608, nickname "Feng San Er Qu") and He Likang (QQ No. 13366338, nickname "Jue Kou Bu Ti De Ai"), as well as records of adding He Likang as a QQ friend, were exported from the QQ "Message Manager";
   ② From the computer hard drive (5JV880RK) seized at Meng Dong's girlfriend's residence, a "Trojan horse" program named "Scout 1.1.rar" and a file named "The day of hanging the horse.txt" were retrieved, containing a large number of QQ numbers and account numbers and passwords for related websites; chat records between Meng Dong and He Likang were exported from the QQ "Message Manager."

18. *QQ Chat Records between Meng Dong and He Liangliang*, proving that:
   ① On the afternoon of July 22, 2005, Meng Dong disclosed to He Liangliang that he had stolen several online sales game point cards which he wanted to sell, but did not know how to do it. He asked He Liangliang to help find He Likang, whereupon He Liangliang sent He Likang's QQ number to Meng Dong;
   ② On the morning of July 23, 2005, Meng Dong stated that he had already received money through online banking from selling stolen Q coins, and that He Likang had earned more than him. He asked He Liangliang to take care of He Likang and tell him to hide for a few days and not go to work at the internet cafe;
   ③ In the evening of August 4, 2005, He Likang borrowed He Liangliang's QQ number to chat with Meng Dong. After indicating that he was borrowing He Liangliang's QQ number, He Likang informed Meng Dong that the Shanghai network surveillance authority had traced the internet cafe where he had been online in Shanxi, and that he had been exposed.

19. *QQ Chat Records between Meng Dong and He Likang*, proving that:
   ① On the afternoon of July 22, 2005, Meng Dong disclosed to He Likang that he had used a Trojan horse program to steal a large number of website account numbers and passwords, and then provided He Likang with the account numbers and passwords of entities such as Tianxiajiayouzhan, Maoli Company, and Shanda Network Online Sales System. After He Likang browsed and discovered that Maoli Company's account contained a large number of Q coins and game point cards, he conspired with Meng Dong to steal and sell them at low prices for profit;
   ② From late night of July 22 to early morning of July 23, 2005, Meng Dong continuously requested He Likang to top up Q coins for the QQ numbers he provided. He Likang informed Meng Dong that he was selling stolen game cards at RMB 3 each. The two also discussed stealing Maoli Company's QQ numbers, topping up membership fees and 100 Q coins for those QQ numbers, and then selling them;
   ③ On the morning of July 23, 2005, in addition to continuing to request He Likang to top up Q coins for the QQ numbers he provided, Meng Dong repeatedly reminded him to leave the internet cafe where he was currently working as soon as possible. He Likang disclosed to Meng Dong that he had already sold the QQ numbers that had been topped up with Q coins. Finally, the two agreed to log off together and requested each other to delete the other's QQ number.

20. *Testimonies of Witness Yin Wei on August 4 and 11, 2005*, proving that on the night and early morning of July 22, 2005, at the request of He Likang, he helped sell some game point cards, receiving over RMB 400. He Likang topped up Q coins for him, applied for membership, paid half a year's membership fee, and also applied for Blue Diamond, Yellow Diamond, etc., using a total of about 380 Q coins.

21. *Testimony of Witness Rong Jie on August 12, 2005*, proving that about 20 days earlier, He Likang gave him 200 Q coins, but a few days later he found that those Q coins were gone.

22. *Testimony of Witness Liu Qiang on August 12, 2005*, proving that around July 20, 2005, He Likang topped up more than 200 Q coins for him. He used 110 that night, but found the remaining Q coins missing on the third day.

23. *Testimonies of Witness Bi Rujun on August 4 and 11, 2005*, proving that one evening in July, before dinner, He Likang claimed he had more than 200,000 Q coins.

24. *Notice of Inquiry into Deposits/Remittances (Receipt) and Attachments*, proving that the account of Card No. 770 opened by Meng Dong with his ID card at the Industrial and Commercial Bank of China, Guangzhou Yiyuan Xincun Sub-branch, had a zero balance before July 22, 2005. From July 22 to 23, a total of 23 transactions occurred, including 19 incoming transactions totaling RMB 98,000 and 4 outgoing transactions totaling RMB 90,400. As of the inquiry date of February 23, 2006, the deposit balance in that account was RMB 7,618.

25. *Photographs of the Crime Scene*, proving that on July 22 and 23, 2005, Meng Dong and He Likang committed their crimes at their respective locations.

26. The in-court testimony of the defendant Meng Dong proved that, in order to steal other people's QQ numbers, he invaded a certain forum website and uploaded a Trojan program, causing the account numbers and passwords of customers logging into the website to be automatically transmitted to his email address. After discovering the account numbers and passwords of four websites including Maoli Company, he immediately informed He Likang of the stolen account numbers and passwords via the internet. He Likang then logged into Maoli Company's mlsoft account and discovered a large number of Q-coins and game point cards within the account. The two agreed that Meng Dong would find buyers and inform He Likang of the buyer's QQ number and the quantity to be purchased, and He Likang would recharge the buyer's QQ number with the stolen Q-coins. The buyer would then transfer the money via the internet into Meng Dong's 770 Peony Card.

27. The in-court testimony of the defendant He Likang proved that, after logging into Maoli Company's mlsoft account using the account number and password provided by Meng Dong, he discovered a large number of Q-coins and game point cards. On one hand, he transferred Q-coins into the QQ numbers designated by Meng Dong; on the other hand, he also recharged Q-coins into his own and his friends' QQ numbers. Additionally, he stole game point cards from the account and sold them for profit or gave them to others.

28. A list of seized items proved that Meng Dong's father, Meng Jiemin, assisted Meng Dong in making restitution of RMB 8,000, and He Likang's mother, Qi Hong, assisted He Likang in making restitution of RMB 26,000.

29. A list of returned items proved that the victim unit, Maoli Company, received full compensation for economic losses amounting to RMB 14,384.33 from the Huangpu Branch of the Shanghai Public Security Bureau on November 11, 2005.

30. The testimony of witness Qi Hong dated August 11, 2005, and the "Work Report" written by investigator Lai Xiaofeng proved that He Likang, accompanied by Qi Hong, voluntarily surrendered to the public security authorities and had acts of meritorious service after surrender.

The issues to be resolved in this case are: 1. Can electronic documents be used as evidence in criminal proceedings? 2. Should virtual property in a network environment be protected by criminal law? 3. How should theft in a network environment be understood? 4. How should the amount of theft in a network environment be determined? 5. How should the criminal form of theft in a network environment be determined?

The Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai opined:

I. Article 42, Paragraph 1 of the Criminal Procedure Law stipulates: "All facts that prove the true circumstances of a case are evidence." Electronic documents differ from traditional physical originals in that they are susceptible to copying, modification, and deletion, and therefore cannot independently perform a proof function based solely on their content. However, if an electronic document is related to the case and can objectively reflect the true circumstances of the case when corroborated by other evidence, and if the electronic document has been lawfully obtained, it may also become evidence in criminal proceedings.

To determine whether a particular electronic document can be used as evidence in criminal proceedings, the first step is to examine whether its source is truthful and lawful. The electronic documents used to prove the facts of this case mainly include: the record proving that a computer user with IP address 202.97.144.230 logged into Tencent's online sales platform mlsoft account, QQ chat records, files retrieved from the computer hard drive, and webpage screenshots. Examining this electronic evidence: the IP address was obtained by Tencent upon the entrustment of the victim unit, Maoli Company; this address was confirmed by the public security authorities, and its user was the employer of the defendant He Likang at the time; the QQ chat records were exported by the public security authorities from the message manager using the QQ number of the defendant Meng Dong; the hacker program and the file containing the victim unit's account number and password were also retrieved by the public security authorities from the hard drives used by Meng Dong, seized from his workplace and his girlfriend; the webpage screenshots for specific time periods were provided respectively by Maoli Company, NetEase Company, and Tencent Company. All this electronic evidence was collected by the judicial authorities in accordance with legal procedures. Examining the content proved by this electronic evidence: the hacker program, the file containing the victim unit's account number and password, and the QQ chat records proved that the corresponding account number and password were stolen by Meng Dong, that Meng Dong informed He Likang of the account number and password, and that the two conspired to steal and sell Maoli Company's Q-coins and game point cards; the webpage screenshots provided respectively by Maoli Company, NetEase Company, and Tencent Company, which corroborate each other, proved that Maoli Company's property was damaged during a specific time period; the IP address proved the user terminal used for the theft, and He Likang was the network administrator of the unit using that terminal during that specific time period, making him a prime suspect. And only He Likang could have known Maoli Company's mlsoft account number and password and used the user terminal with IP address 202.97.144.230 to commit the theft, excluding others. Although none of this electronic evidence alone could prove the facts of the case, when corroborated with relevant witness testimony, the transaction records of Meng Dong's 770 Peony Card, and other evidence, it can lead to an exclusive conclusion. After excluding reasonable doubt and being corroborated by other evidence, electronic documents can be included in the chain of evidence as proof of the facts of the case.

II. Q-coins and game point cards are virtual currencies and vouchers issued online by Tencent Company and NetEase Company and constitute virtual property in the network environment. After a user purchases Q-coins and game point cards with real currency, they can obtain equivalent online services provided by the network company that issued the Q-coins and game point cards. Therefore, Q-coins and game point cards reflect the labor value of the network services provided by the network company. The victim unit, Maoli Company, is an agent and reseller of Q-coins and game point cards. It obtains Q-coins and game point cards from Tencent Company and NetEase Company by paying real currency at a discount as stipulated in the contract. The Q-coins and game point cards obtained by Maoli Company after paying the consideration are not only virtual property in the network environment but also represent property that Maoli Company actually enjoys in real life and should be protected by criminal law.

III. Article 2 of the Criminal Law stipulates: "The task of the Criminal Law of the People's Republic of China is to fight against all criminal acts with punishment to safeguard national security, to defend the regime of the people's democratic dictatorship and the socialist system, to protect state property and property collectively owned by the working masses, to protect citizens' privately owned property, to protect citizens' personal rights, democratic rights, and other rights, and to maintain social order and economic order, ensuring the smooth progress of socialist construction." The criminal acts referred to in the Criminal Law are acts that occur in real life, and the property to be protected by the Criminal Law is also property in real life. The network environment is a virtualization of real life, and it is replete with a large number of virtual acts such as murder, fighting, robbery, and theft that are prohibited by law in real life. If virtual acts in the network environment do not harm the objects protected by the Criminal Law in real life, they are not acts that need to be regulated by the Criminal Law. However, if virtual acts cause harm to the objects protected by the Criminal Law in real life and constitute a crime, they should be subject to criminal punishment. Article 264 of the Criminal Law stipulates: "Whoever steals public or private property in a relatively large amount or repeatedly steals shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not more than three years, criminal detention, or public surveillance and shall also, or shall only, be fined; if the amount is huge or there are other serious circumstances, the offender shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than three years but not more than ten years and shall also be fined; if the amount is especially huge or there are other especially serious circumstances, the offender shall be sentenced to fixed-term imprisonment of not less than ten years or life imprisonment and shall also be fined or have property confiscated; in any of the following circumstances, the offender shall be sentenced to life imprisonment or death and shall also have property confiscated: (1) stealing property from a financial institution, where the amount is especially huge; (2) stealing precious cultural relics, where the circumstances are serious." The defendants Meng Dong and He Likang, with the purpose of illegal possession, committed acts online of invading Maoli Company's account and secretly stealing Q-coins and game point cards. This act infringed upon the property rights of Maoli Company that are protected by criminal law in real life, undoubtedly constitutes the crime of theft, and should be subject to criminal punishment.

IV. The amount is a key factor in determining guilt and sentencing for the crime of theft. There is currently no clear regulation on how to calculate the amount of theft for secretly stealing Q-coins and game point cards online.

Network users can obtain Q-coins and game point cards not only by purchasing them with real currency but also through continuous "cultivation" in online games. This latter method of acquisition makes the price of Q-coins and game point cards ambiguous. As previously mentioned, the purpose of network companies issuing Q-coins and game point cards online is to collect payment from network users for the online services they provide. Q-coins and game point cards reflect the labor value of the network services provided by the network company. Therefore, the amount of property corresponding to Q-coins and game point cards in real life can be determined by their actual transaction price in real life. As for the Q-coins and game point cards obtained by network users through continuous "cultivation" in online games, this is merely a means used by network companies to attract customers. Since this portion of Q-coins and game point cards does not participate in the exchange between the network company and network users, it does not affect the transaction price of Q-coins and game point cards.

There are several transaction prices for Q-coins and game point cards in real life: 1. The sales price listed online by the network company; 2. The price formed by network users trading with each other offline; 3. The transaction price between the network company and its agents; etc. Specifically in this case, the actual transaction price between the network company and the agent should be used to determine the amount of property corresponding to the stolen Q-coins and game point cards in real life. This is because when an actor commits theft, the victim's property generally suffers a corresponding loss, and the amount of theft is closely related to the property loss suffered by the victim. After all, only public or private property in real life that is harmed by criminal acts is the object protected by criminal law. In this case, using the exchange price agreed upon in the contract between the victim unit Maoli Company and Tencent Company and NetEase Company to calculate the amount of property represented by the stolen Q-coins and game point cards in real life can accurately reflect the property loss suffered by Maoli Company. Under the current circumstances where there is no clear regulation on how to calculate the amount of theft for Q-coins and game point cards, the indictment did not calculate based on the publicly recognized selling price of Q-coins and game point cards online but instead determined the theft amount based on the actual price paid by Maoli Company upon purchase. This is not only reasonable but also supported by sufficient evidence and should be upheld. The amount of property corresponding to the stolen Q-coins and game point cards in real life in this case does not require a price appraisal by an authoritative institution. (Editor's note: According to Article 5(1)(1) of the Supreme People's Court's Interpretation on Several Issues Concerning the Specific Application of Law in Adjudicating Theft Cases, for commodities in the traditional circulation field, the theft amount is calculated based on the medium market retail price.)

V. The defendants Meng Dong and He Likang stole Q-coins from the victim unit, Maoli Company, via the internet. After discovering the theft, Maoli Company promptly notified the issuing unit, Tencent Company. Tencent Company, through a method of sealing and freezing online, assisted Maoli Company in recovering 15,019 Q-coins. Defense counsel argued that this portion of recovered Q-coins constituted an attempted crime and should be subject to a mitigated punishment according to law.

Article 23 of the Criminal Law stipulates: "An attempt to commit a crime is one where the offender has already started to commit the crime but failed to complete it due to reasons independent of the offender's will." The standard for identifying attempted theft has long been subject to various theoretical views, such as the contact theory, the transfer theory, the concealment theory, the loss theory, the loss of control theory, and the control theory. This is because the target of the crime of theft is a wide variety of public and private property, and different types of property theft will lead to different methods for determining whether the crime is completed or attempted. In judicial practice, there is no single standard for determining attempted theft in a specific case. The determination of whether a crime is completed or attempted can only be made based on the three conditions stipulated by law—"started to commit the crime," "failed to complete the crime," and "failure to complete the crime is due to reasons independent of the offender's will"—combined with the type of property stolen.

The Q-coins controlled by the victim unit, Maoli Company, correspond to the property that the company enjoys in real life. The defendants Meng Dong and He Likang stole Q-coins from Maoli Company via the internet with the intention of illegally appropriating the property in real life corresponding to these Q-coins. The facts of this case prove that after He Likang started to commit the secret theft, the Q-coins instantly left the control of Maoli Company and reached the accounts of buyers designated by Meng Dong. Meng Dong received the buyers' remittances on his 770 Peony Card. At this point, the theft by the two individuals was completed, and the purpose of illegal possession they intended to achieve through this act was also achieved. Therefore, the crime should be determined as completed. As for He Likang transferring some Q-coins to his own and friends' accounts, this is a matter of disposal of the proceeds of crime; Tencent Company's recovery of 15,019 Q-coins online through sealing and freezing is a means for the victim unit to recover property losses. Neither of these is related to the criminal form of the two individuals.

In conclusion, the Q-coins and game point cards in the account of the victim unit, Maoli Company, as a distributor for Tencent Company and NetEase Company, correspond to the property it enjoys in real life. Once stolen, the owner loses all property rights of possession, use, benefit, and disposal over this property. The defendants Meng Dong and He Likang, with the purpose of illegal possession, jointly stole Q-coins and game point cards worth RMB 25,948.96 from Maoli Company via the internet, infringing upon Maoli Company's property rights and constituting the crime of theft with a huge amount. The facts of the crime of theft against Meng Dong and He Likang charged by the prosecutorial authority are clear, the evidence is conclusive and sufficient, and the charge is established. Criminal punishment should be imposed on Meng Dong and He Likang according to law. Meng Dong and He Likang are first-time and occasional offenders. After being brought to justice, they truthfully confessed their criminal facts. With the assistance of their family members, they made full restitution for Maoli Company's losses. Furthermore, He Likang also had circumstances of voluntary surrender and meritorious service. They may all be given a lighter punishment according to law. The defense counsel's opinion that the two defendants' criminal circumstances are relatively minor, that they genuinely confessed and repented, and that a suspended sentence may be applied according to law should be adopted. Accordingly, the Huangpu District People's Court of Shanghai rendered the judgment on June 26, 2006:

1. The defendant Meng Dong is convicted of theft and sentenced to three years' imprisonment, suspended for three years, and fined RMB 3,000.

2. The defendant He Likang is convicted of theft and sentenced to one year and six months' imprisonment, suspended for one year and six months, and fined RMB 2,000.

3. The two computer hard drives and the 770 Peony Card used by the defendant Meng Dong for the crime, which are seized in the case, are confiscated.

After the first-instance judgment was pronounced, the defendants Meng Dong and He Likang did not file an appeal within the statutory period, and the prosecutorial authority did not file a protest. The first-instance judgment became legally effective.
